title: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES
alt_titles: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES, WITH OR WITHOUT MICROCORNEA

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cataract-2 of multiple types (CTRCT2), with or without microcornea, is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC; 123680) on chromosome 2q33.

checks.claim: Cataract-2 of multiple types (CTRCT2), with or without microcornea, is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC).
checks.evidence_quote: Further analysis of the original Coppock-like-cataract family identified a missense mutation in a highly conserved segment of exon 2 of CRYGC.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports a CRYGC missense mutation causing cataract in one Coppock-like family. It does not mention heterozygosity, multiple cataract types or microcornea; these are not in the abstract.

checks.claim: The CRYGC gene is located on chromosome 2q33.
checks.evidence_quote: We recently mapped the aculeiform cataract to the gamma-crystallin locus (CRYG) on chromosome 2q33-35
checks.explanation: The abstract places the CRYG gene cluster, which includes CRYGC, on 2q33-35. Giving CRYGC's location as 2q33 is standard nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: CTRCT2 is an autosomal dominant congenital cataract caused by mutation in the CRYGC gene. Families with CRYGC mutations have had Coppock-like cataract, highly variable zonular pulverulent cataract, or nuclear congenital cataract. In some families the nuclear cataract occurred with microcornea, nystagmus, and amblyopia.

paragraphs.text: Scott et al. (1994) described a 7-generation family in which 48 of 138 individuals were known to have autosomal dominant congenital cataracts of the pulverulent type. Twenty-eight of the 53 individuals examined had congenital cataracts: in 19 the cataract was unilateral (8 right eyes and 11 left eyes) and in 9 it was bilateral. When historic data were included, the 48 affected members comprised 28 with unilateral cataract, 17 with bilateral cataract, and 3 obligate carriers who were not examined. Whether the cataract was unilateral or bilateral appeared to be random. In patients with unilateral cataract, detailed slit-lamp examination of the clinically unaffected eye showed no lens opacity. Severity ranged from a subtle unilateral zonular cataract with 20/20 visual acuity, through bilateral inner fetal nuclear pulverulent opacities with 20/16 visual acuity in both eyes, to dense unilateral and bilateral nuclear cataracts that required early surgical removal.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2009) studied a 4-generation family from northern China with 6 members who had nuclear cataracts and microcornea. The affected individuals had bilateral congenital nuclear cataracts, with a central nuclear opacity affecting the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nucleus of the lens. They also had congenitally small eyeballs and corneas with a diameter of approximately 9 to 10 mm. Every affected individual had the same poor visual acuity of hand movement in front of the eye, and all had nystagmus and amblyopia.

paragraphs.text: Guo et al. (2012) described a 4-generation Chinese family with isolated bilateral autosomal dominant nuclear cataracts and microcornea. The opacities involved the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nuclei, and the corneal diameter was approximately 9 mm. All patients had nystagmus and amblyopia, intraocular pressure was normal, and there were no systemic abnormalities. The male proband (II:7) was diagnosed with bilateral nuclear cataract and microcornea at age 8 years and underwent iridectomy on both eyes at that age. At age 38, his left eye underwent phacoemulsification and intraocular lens implantation. Individual I:2 was examined at age 68 years, and individual II:2 was diagnosed at age 13 years. Individual III:3 had cataract extraction at 6 years of age. Individuals III:6 and IV:1 were first diagnosed at 6 months and 1 year of age, respectively.

paragraphs.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance of CTRCT2 was reported by Lubsen et al. (1987), who noted that the cataract in their family occurred in heterozygotes. It was also reported in multigenerational families by Scott et al. (1994), Ren et al. (2000), Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007), Zhang et al. (2009), Li et al. (2012), and Guo et al. (2012).

checks.evidence_quote: a family in which a hereditary Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus occurs in heterozygotes
checks.explanation: The abstract says the cataract occurs in heterozygotes, which implies dominant inheritance. It never uses the words 'autosomal dominant' or the name CTRCT2.

checks.claim: Autosomal dominant inheritance of CTRCT2 was reported in multigenerational families by Scott et al. (1994), Ren et al. (2000), Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007), Zhang et al. (2009), Li et al. (2012), and Guo et al. (2012).

paragraphs.text: In a family with a hereditary Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus, Lubsen et al. (1987) found that the cataract locus was closely linked to the gamma-crystallin gene cluster, with a maximum lod score of 7.58 at theta = 0. A gamma-crystallin haplotype (P) was found only in family members with cataract, and all family members with cataract carried it. Lubsen et al. (1987) concluded that the primary cause of a human cataract could possibly be a lesion in a crystallin gene.

checks.explanation: The paper writes the recombination fraction as phi and the draft writes theta. Both are notations for the same value, 0.

paragraphs.text: Brakenhoff et al. (1994) cloned the gamma-D and pseudo-gamma-E genes from the Coppock-like cataract chromosome of the family studied by Lubsen et al. (1987). The gamma-D gene was functionally equivalent to the wildtype allele. The pseudo-gamma-E gene, however, had a cluster of sequence changes in and around its TATA box. Together these changes increased promoter activity 10-fold, raising expression of the pseudogene to 30% of that of gamma-D.

paragraphs.text: Héon et al. (1999) re-examined the original Coppock-like cataract family and identified a missense mutation in a highly conserved segment of exon 2 of the CRYGC gene. The mutation was not seen in a large control population. They found that the CRYGE pseudogene change reported earlier as the Coppock-like cataract mutation was a polymorphism present in 23% of their controls. They noted that, to date, there was no direct evidence that upregulation of a pseudogene causes cataracts. Héon et al. (1999) concluded that their findings were the first evidence that CRYGC is involved in human cataract formation.

paragraphs.text: In a 7-generation family with autosomal dominant zonular pulverulent cataract, Ren et al. (2000) identified a heterozygous 5-bp duplication in exon 2 of the CRYGC gene. The duplication was present in each affected family member and absent from unaffected family members and from unaffected controls. Ren et al. (2000) found that activation of the pseudo-gamma-E-crystallin gene was unlikely to cause the cataracts in this family: base changes in its TATA box were also found in unaffected controls, which excluded them as a sole cause. The CRYGD gene showed no abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) sequenced the CRYGA-D gene cluster in a family with nuclear congenital cataract. In affected members they identified a heterozygous c.502C-T transition in the CRYGC gene, resulting in an arg168-to-trp (R168W) substitution. The mutation segregated with cataract. Healthy family members and 170 unrelated controls had a normal sequence. Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) concluded that R168W, which was listed as a SNP in the NCBI database, is a disease-causing mutation and should no longer be considered a SNP.

paragraphs.text: In a 4-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea, Zhang et al.
